messages.subject: Re: triangular matrix views
parts:
I'm returning this discussion to stan-dev.
Replies inline.

On 12/4/12 4:24 PM, Yuanjun Gao wrote:
> Dear Bob,
>
> I attached my code and the method I use for leapfrog and covariance matrix estimation in the E-mail. What I have done is :
> 1. Added a function "nondiag_leapfrog" in "stan/mcmc/util.hpp" to implement the leapfrog with a matrix
> 2. Added the file in stan/mcmc/nuts_nondiag.hpp to implement the sampler class for nondiag matrix
> 3. Modified "stan/gm/command.hpp" by adding an option "--nondiag_matrix" and writing the corresponding item in "--help".
> By adding this option, the sampler "nuts_nondiag" will be called.

> So to use my sampler, just do
>
> ./bernoulli --nondiag_mass --data=bernoulli.Rdata

Perfect -- that's exactly what we'd sketched out, so I'm glad
it was workable.

> Thank you for your information about trangularView. Since I am using the Cholesky decomposition of the mass matrix, I
> think it will help the program a lot. I guess it can also be used in estimating covariance by saving half of the
> computation. But since I will have exams in the following weeks, my work on that may be quite slow
>
> Right now the thing that is bothering me is that in order to implement the leapfrog method, I have to use the location
> and momentum parameters, which are of the type vectors instead of matrix. Right now I solve it by using
> "Eigen::Map<Eigen::MatrixXd>" to solve the problem. Which means that for each leapfrog, I'll have to create three
> matrix. This is basically what I didï¿½
>
> //The nondiagonal leapfrog implemented
> double nondiag_leapfrog(stan::model::prob_grad& model,
> std::vector<int> z,
> const Eigen::MatrixXd& _cov_L,
> std::vector<double>& x, std::vector<double>& m,
> std::vector<double>& g, double epsilon,
> std::ostream* error_msgs = 0,
> std::ostream* output_msgs = 0) {
> Eigen::Map<Eigen::MatrixXd> x_mat(x.data(),x.size(),1);
> Eigen::Map<Eigen::MatrixXd> m_mat(m.data(),m.size(),1);
> Eigen::Map<Eigen::MatrixXd> g_mat(g.data(),g.size(),1);
> ï¿½ï¿½ï¿½
> }
>
> I think this is where the inefficiency lies, but I am not sure how to improve it since I am not familiar with the
> interface of Eigen with other data structure in C++. Could you help me with that?

The way to answer questions about which part of the code's
inefficient, you need a profiler. In general, the compiler is
so clever that it's pretty much impossible for humans to tell
what's going to be efficient, except at a very coarse level.
For more information on C++ optimization, you could start with this
(book length) survey:

http://www.agner.org/optimize/optimizing_cpp.pdf

The Eigen implementation uses expression templates, which can
be a bit subtle to optimize. Here's the general story on Map:

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TutorialMapClass.html

You need to track memory allocation and copy operations.
When you do this:

Eigen::Map<Eigen::MatrixXd> x_mat(x.data(),x.size(),1);

it will construct an instance of Eigen::Map. But
it doesn't copy any data or do any allocation (except on the
function call stack -- the heap allocation with malloc or
new is what's expensive).

The map just holds a pointer to the underlying data. Then when it's
used, it reads from the mapped data rather than its own data. This
can have a bit of overhead from the constructor call, but it's only
a couple operations -- that is, you shouldn't notice the time it takes.

The one thing to watch out for is copies, which will happen if
you ever try to assign the map to a regular matrix or return it
in a function that returns a matrix:

std::vector<double> v = ...;
Map<VectorXd> v_map(&v[0],v.size()); // no alloc, no elt copy
VectorXd v_copy = v_map; // alloc, elt copies

Note that we can't use C++11 features due to restrictions from R
and CRAN (they're way way behind the times), so you can't use the
std::vector .data() method. Instead, you need to do this:

Eigen::Map<Eigen::MatrixXd> x_mat(&x[0],x.size(),1);

the &x[0] will create a reference to the start of the matrix (same
behavior, uglier syntax).

For efficiency, Eigen specializes the template for matrices to
templates for vectors and row vectors:

matrix: Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic> == MatrixXd
column vector: Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> == VectorXd
row vector: Matrix<double,1,Dynamic> == RowVectorXd

So you probably want to map vectors (or row vectors depending
on usage) rather than matrices, as in this:

Map<VectorXd> x_mat(&x[0],x.size());

or RowVectorXd, depending on how it will be used
The reference to x[0], "&x[0]", will do the same thing
as .data() in a much uglier way -- return the pointer to the
initial point in the data array.

The other thing we could do is just replace the std::vector with
an Eigen vector. That'd probably be more efficient in that it
doesn't even need the lightweight view wrapper. The only reason it's
std::vector now is that we wrote the first version before
the matrix lib!

- Bob


> On Dec 4, 2012, at 3:29 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
>
>> http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/QuickRefPage.html#QuickRef_DiagTriSymm
>>
>> If M is a lower triangular matrix, replace the use of
>> M in arithmetic/solver operations with:
>>
>> M.triangularView<Eigen::Lower>()
>>
>> In cases where the type of M is templated (you probably won't
>> need this), you'd write:
>>
>> M.template triangularView<Eigen::Lower>()
>>
>> If M is symmetric, replace uses of it with:
>>
>> M.selfAdjointView<Eigen::Lower>()
>>
>> This treats the upper triangle as matching the lower triangle
>> and speeds up operations in the same way that triangular does.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>
>>
>>

On 12/4/12 8:38 PM, Yuanjun Gao wrote:
> Dear Bob,
>

> Thank you so much for your comprehensive answer. I have thought about changing all the std::vec to matrix vector, but it seems that a lot of efforts will be taken to do that. I will think more about that.

It wouldn't be too much work because they
pretty much share all the concepts we care about
(allocation constructors, resizing, indexing/setting).

Another motivation for the original design is that it
produces (or can produce) models that don't depend on
Eigen. But given that most of the things we do including
vectorization now rely on Eigen, I don't think restricting
the model interfaces to std::vector buys us anything in
terms of portability.

- Bob

P.S. Yuanjun: please reply to the stan-dev list for discussions
about Stan development.
